title: Pfitzinger Marathon Training Plans Explained
excerpt: How Pfitzinger's Advanced Marathoning plans work: mileage tiers (55 to 85+), 12 vs 18 weeks, weekly structure, who each suits, and where to get them.
body:
Pfitzinger Marathon Training Plans Explained

Pete Pfitzinger's marathon training plans, published in Advanced Marathoning (co-written with Scott Douglas), are built for experienced marathoners who already run around 35 miles (56 km) a week or more and want a demanding, structured build. This page explains how the plans are organised, what a typical week contains, which tier suits which runner, and where to get the actual schedules. We don't reproduce the book's schedules. You'll need the book for those.

Comparing different marathon plans? See them side by side here.

Who Pete Pfitzinger is

Pfitzinger won the 1984 US Olympic Marathon Trials in 2:11:43. At the Los Angeles Olympics that year he finished 11th in 2:13:53, the top American. He made the team again in 1988, placing 3rd at the Trials, and finished 14th in Seoul in 2:14:44. He later worked as an exercise physiologist and coach, and that background shows in how the plans explain the purpose of each workout. Advanced Marathoning is now in its fourth edition, published in 2025.

How the plans are organised

Each plan is named by its length and peak weekly mileage. "18/55", for example, means 18 weeks long, peaking at 55 miles (89 km) a week. The book offers plans at several mileage levels:

  • Up to 55 miles (89 km) a week
  • 55–70 miles (89–113 km) a week
  • 70–85 miles (113–137 km) a week
  • 85+ miles (137+ km) a week

Each level comes in 18-week and 12-week versions. The book also covers running several marathons in one season. Check the current edition for the exact plans available, because details have changed between editions. For example, the fourth edition moved to time-based threshold sessions.

What a typical Pfitzinger week looks like

The schedules use a small set of workout types, each with a defined purpose:

  • Long run: the weekly long run, typically on the weekend, at a steady aerobic pace. Some long runs include a block at marathon pace.
  • Medium-long run: a second, shorter long run in the middle of the week. This is a signature feature of the plans: it adds endurance without a second weekend-length run.
  • Lactate-threshold session: sustained running at a comfortably hard effort, roughly the pace you could race for about an hour.
  • VO2max intervals: repeats at about 5K race effort, used mainly in the later phases.
  • General aerobic and recovery runs: the rest of the week. Recovery runs are meant to be genuinely slow.

A typical week has one long run, one medium-long run and one or two quality sessions, with general aerobic and recovery runs in between. The higher tiers add more running days and, eventually, some days with two runs. Across the 18 weeks the plans move through phases: endurance first, then threshold work, then race-specific preparation, then a taper of about three weeks.

Which tier suits which runner

These are general guidelines. The book gives its own entry requirements for each plan.

  • Up to 55 miles: a good first Pfitzinger plan if you have run a marathon and comfortably manage 30–40 miles (48–64 km) a week. It is the most common entry point.
  • 55–70 miles: for runners who have done a 55-mile peak without problems and want more volume. It usually means six or seven running days a week.
  • 70–85 and 85+ miles: for highly experienced, high-mileage runners, often chasing competitive times. These plans include days with two runs.
  • 12-week versions: for runners who are already fit and running near the plan's early mileage, for example after a recent race. If you're building from a lower base, the 18-week version is the safer choice.

Strengths and drawbacks

Strengths: every run has a clear purpose, and marathon-specific work is built into the long runs. The progression is well thought out, and the book explains the physiology behind it, so you can adapt the plans sensibly.

Drawbacks: the mileage is high, even at the entry tier, and the medium-long runs add up. There is little cross-training. Runners who skip ahead to a tier above their experience often get injured or overtired.

Where to get the plans

The full day-by-day schedules are in Advanced Marathoning by Pete Pfitzinger and Scott Douglas (Human Kinetics, 4th edition, 2025). We recommend buying the book rather than relying on copies online. The book explains how to pace each workout and how to adjust the plans if you miss training, and the schedules only make sense with that context.

Not running 35+ miles a week yet? Build up with our 18-week intermediate plan, which peaks at 55 miles. Or, for a first marathon, start with the guide to choosing a marathon plan.

FAQ

Is Pfitzinger good for beginners?

No. The plans assume you have run at least one marathon and already run about 30–40 miles a week. First-timers should use a lower-mileage plan and come to Pfitzinger for a later race.

What's the difference between Pfitzinger 18/55 and 18/70?

Both are 18 weeks long. 18/55 peaks at 55 miles (89 km) a week, and 18/70 peaks at 70 miles (113 km). In practice, 18/70 means more running days, longer medium-long runs and more total volume. It's a step to take after completing a 55-mile plan successfully.

Should I choose the 12-week or the 18-week Pfitzinger plan?

Choose the 18-week plan unless you are already fit and running close to the plan's early weekly mileage. The 12-week plans compress the build and leave little room for missed training.

Can I follow Pfitzinger in kilometres?

Yes. Convert each distance (1 mile = 1.609 km) and round sensibly. The structure and paces stay the same.

  2. Pfitzinger, P., & Douglas, S. (2025). Advanced Marathoning (4th ed.). Human Kinetics. https://canada.humankinetics.com/products/advanced-marathoning-4th-edition
  3. Road Trail Run. (2025). Book review: Advanced Marathoning, 4th edition. https://www.roadtrailrun.com/2025/12/roadtrailread-book-review-advanced.html
keyTakeaway: Pfitzinger's plans suit experienced marathoners already running 30-40+ miles a week; start at the lowest tier that fits, and get the full schedules from Advanced Marathoning.
